overview.text: Bullfighting, or tauromachy, is a public spectacle best known as a Spanish tradition, with a related history in parts of Latin America. In the Spanish-style corrida de toros, a matador and assistants face a bull in a ring through a set sequence of events. First, the bull is drawn with a cape and confronted by mounted picadors; next, banderilleros place decorated barbed sticks; finally, the matador uses a smaller cloth called a muleta and usually kills the bull with a sword. The formal stages, specialized roles, costumes and audience rituals distinguish a corrida from an ordinary contest. Bullfighting has also influenced Spanish art and literature, though its meaning and acceptance vary among people.

key_facts.text: A corrida begins with a parade called the paseíllo; its three main phases are the tercio de varas, tercio de banderillas and tercio de muerte.
The matador leads the performance, assisted by picadors on horseback and banderilleros on foot.
In the final phase, the matador performs a sequence of passes with the muleta and typically uses a sword to kill the bull.
Bullfighting is strongly associated with Spain, and the tradition also has a long history in parts of Latin America.
Madrid’s tourism guide connects bullfighting with works by artists and writers including Goya, Picasso and Lorca.
